answer.evidence: The main body is the crossbeam (rows 9-17) between two posts. Its top is at best a 2-3 row band (rows 10-12). That band is the same brown as the face below it (L about 109 in rows 10-11 and 13-14), and row 12 is a broken decorative stripe with rivets rather than a continuous front-edge line. The beam therefore reads mostly as a front-facing strip with a shadow below it. The posts have only a narrow 5-row cap (rows 4-8, 12-14 px wide) with a corner highlight, and then run as vertical faces from row 9 to row 46. They show no ellipse, no front-edge line and no eave shadow. The gate leaves (rows 19-45) are flat vertical panels. The whole drawing is a flat front elevation with no real top surfaces, not the 'seen from above' view the name describes.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse prop, so I judged it by eye against the reference as well as by the numbers. Its primary facts match or beat the references: 16 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels. That means the outlines carry a tint, brown beside the wood and dark red or blue beside the metal, rather than a uniform black sticker line. The posts show a cap highlight, a mid tone, a dark side and rust or rivet speckle. The crossbeam reads as a wood-like surface with its own highlight and shadow, and the corrugated leaves have ribbing and weathering dots. There are no large flat fills. The weak points are the total of 20 distinct colours across several materials, which gives about 4 steps per ramp against the references' 5-6, and the small size, which leaves the piece slightly thinner than a full house. These are mild enough that a careful artist would accept it next to the references without it looking like a flat sticker.

The crossbeam (rows 9-17) shows rows 10-11 and 13-14 in nearly the same brown (L≈109-118). The light tan line at row 12 looks like a decorative stud strip, not a top-surface edge. The darkening at rows 15-17 is shading on the front face, not eave shadow under a top. At most about 3 rows could be read as a beam top. The gate leaves are drawn as vertical panels on the sides, with no visible horizontal surface, so the whole object reads as a front elevation rather than a 3/4 view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse prop, so I judged it by eye as well as by the measured facts. The facts favour it: 16 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10 for the references, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline carries a tint. By eye the outline is dark brown beside the wood and dark rust or blue-grey beside the metal leaves, not a uniform black line. The posts and caps show a few distinct steps (cap highlight, face, shadow side, rust streaks). The corrugated leaves show ridge banding, and the crossbeam has a central block with some grain. Weaknesses: only about 4 steps per material against the references' 5-6, a very small total palette (20 colours), and a slightly thin, simple look next to the shingled roofs. There are no large flat fills, and it would sit acceptably beside the references without looking like a sticker.
